---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- The prophecy is written as a funeral song (a *kinah*), sung as though Israel's end had already come. This shows both how certain the judgment is and how Amos feels about it. (PUL)
- Gill says it is the Lord's word, not Amos's own, and must be heard even though it is against them. (GILL)
- Matthew Henry says we need to hear warning words as well as comforting ones. (MH)

**v. 2**
- "Virgin" is a poetic female picture of the nation, suggesting grace and beauty. Israel is not wiped out as a people, but she is ended as a nation. "Forsaken" is better translated "dashed to the earth." (ELL)
- The Pulpit Commentary says "virgin" means tenderly guarded, not morally pure. "No more rise" refers to the northern kingdom of ten tribes, which was never set up again. (PUL)
- Gill suggests the title may be ironic, given Israel's calf-worship. He says neither her idols nor the God she left would lift her up. (GILL)
- Guzik pictures a helpless young woman with no one coming to help her. (EW)

**v. 3**
- Cities will be cut to a tenth in the coming war with Assyria. (ELL)
- This happens to small towns as well as large ones. (PUL)

**v. 4**
- Seeking God is rewarded by finding him, and that is life in the fullest sense. (ELL)
- The Pulpit Commentary reads it as a command and its reward: "Seek me, and so live." (PUL)
- Gill says that even with judgment announced, hope is held out if they repent. (GILL)
- Guzik notes they could only seek God by giving up the rival places of worship. (EW)

**v. 5**
- Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba once had a rich spiritual history. Bethel is where God met Jacob, Gilgal is where Israel's shame was "rolled away" under Joshua, and Beersheba is linked to the patriarchs. They had become places of empty worship. (EW)
- The verse contains a pun that English can't carry over: *ha-Gilgal galoh yigleh*. One rendering is "Roll-town shall be rolled away." "Bethel" (house of God) will become *aven*, "nothingness" (compare Hosea's name "Beth-aven"). (PUL; also SL5, where Clarke gives the same reading)
- Beersheba's fate isn't mentioned because it lay outside the northern kingdom. (PUL)
- Henry: God isn't truly sought unless he is sought alone, because he tolerates no rivals. (MH)

**v. 6**
- "House of Joseph" means the northern kingdom. (ELL)
- Mercy is mixed with judgment here: the threat still depends on how they respond. (ELL)
- The fire recalls God as "a consuming fire" (Deut. 4:24). (PUL)

**v. 7**
- Justice, which should be sweet, is turned into bitter wormwood. (PUL, quoting Jerome)
- Righteousness is thrown to the ground through false verdicts. (ELL)
- Ellicott notes that Pusey saw here a picture of Christ being humiliated. (ELL)
- Gill says the verse is aimed at kings and judges. (GILL)

**v. 8**
- In a world full of nature-worship, this verse declares that Israel's God rules the whole universe. (ELL)
- The Pulpit Commentary contrasts "he that maketh" with "ye who turn" in v. 7. It sees God here as the moral ruler of the world, and reads the poured-out waters as pointing to the Flood and similar judgments. (PUL)
- Gill reports that some read the verse as being about Christ. (GILL)
- Guzik: God is strong enough to save and strong enough to judge. (EW)

**v. 9**
- Ellicott suggests the sense is "who makes destruction flash upon the strong." (ELL)
- The Pulpit Commentary gives a similar sense: like lightning, and no fortress is safe. (PUL)
- Guzik: if fortresses can't stand before God, no one can. (EW)

**v. 10**
- The "gate" was the city's law court. (EW)
- The one who rebukes there may be a judge, a chief or a prophet. (PUL)
- Gill thinks the corrupt judges hated prophets like Amos. (GILL)
- Henry says they couldn't stand the sight of an honest man. (MH)

**v. 11**
- "Burdens of wheat" are payments forced from the poor. They may have been a disguised form of the interest the Law forbade (Exod. 22:25). (PUL)
- Houses of cut stone were a mark of luxury. Losing them carries out the curse of Deuteronomy 28:30. (PUL)
- Guzik: what the wicked gained by oppression would only be temporary. (EW)

**v. 12**
- The "bribe" was probably a ransom the poor had to pay to escape a harsh sentence. (ELL)
- The Pulpit Commentary says the poor got no justice unless they could pay for it. (PUL)

**v. 13**
- In an evil time the sensible person stays silent. Even so, the prophet himself can't keep quiet. (PUL)
- Calvin reads it as people being afraid to speak under tyranny. (CAL)
- Ellicott sees the silence itself as a curse on the people. (ELL)

**v. 14**
- The people assumed God was always with them because of the covenant, and their prosperity under King Jeroboam II seemed to prove it. In fact God's help depended on their obedience. (PUL)
- Ellicott calls vv. 14–15 "a beam of sunshine": the doom can still be avoided. (ELL)
- Gill reads "good" as God himself, and Christ. (GILL)

**v. 15**
- Hating and loving go deeper than simply seeking. "Remnant" shows that only a few will be spared. (PUL)
- Gill links this to the faithful remnant in every age. (GILL)

**v. 16**
- Farmers will have to be called in as mourners. Guzik suggests there won't be enough professional mourners, and that Amos the farmer naturally thinks in farming terms. (EW)
- Ellicott says the disaster will be universal. (ELL)

**v. 17**
- "Pass through" echoes the night of Passover, when God "passed through" Egypt. This time God will not pass over Israel. (PUL; ELL)

**v. 18**
- The people longed for "the Day of the LORD," expecting it to defeat their enemies. They ignored that it depended on their own moral state. (PUL)
- The Pulpit Commentary also notes that to Christian readers the phrase looks ahead to the final judgment. (PUL)
- Ellicott: "There is a dark side to the pillar of fire." (ELL)

**v. 19**
- They will escape one disaster only to fall into a worse one. (ELL)
- Guzik, quoting Hubbard: darkness and light here mean disaster and safety, not wickedness and goodness. (EW)

**v. 20**
- "Very dark" is the word used of the plague of darkness in Egypt (Exod. 10:22). (ELL)

**vv. 21–22**
- Mere ritual, without righteousness and real repentance, is condemned. (ELL)
- Barnes notes that "I will not smell" echoes Leviticus 26:31. (BAR)
- Guzik compares Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:23–24. (EW)

**v. 23**
- The sound of their songs was a burden to God. Ellicott compares Jesus cleansing the Temple. (ELL)

**v. 24**
- "Ever-flowing" means a stream that never dries up. (ELL; BAR)
- Barnes pictures justice that no bribe can turn aside. (BAR)
- Guzik, quoting McComiskey: justice can't be a short burst; it has to keep flowing all year. (EW)

**vv. 25–26**
- Ellicott calls these "one of the most difficult" passages in the Old Testament. Is the question expecting "no"? Is v. 26 about the past ("you carried") or the future ("you shall carry," into exile)? (ELL)
- Ellicott himself prefers the future reading, while noting that most commentators read it as past. (ELL)
- He says "Kaiwan" (Chiun) stands for the planet Saturn. Stephen's quotation in Acts 7:43 follows the Greek Septuagint, which reads "Rephan." (ELL)
- Guzik says these were pagan gods Israel brought out of Egypt. He notes that the Septuagint reads "Moloch" and "Rephan," and that the NIV translates the names as "shrine" and "pedestal." (EW)

**v. 27**
- Severe sin merits severe correction: exile. (EW)
- Ellicott reads it as God putting them back under the discipline of wandering, this time in exile. (ELL)

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

- **v. 5, Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin uses this verse to argue that true religion and idolatry can't be combined. God has set a rule for how he is to be worshipped and won't accept human inventions mixed in; Calvin applies this to the Papacy. Turning to God is only real when people give up their superstitions. (CAL)
- **v. 14, Brethren (William Kelly):** Kelly argues against a teaching that he says leaves people uncertain about whether Israel will be restored. He insists that if God's word could fail regarding Israel, it couldn't be trusted for believers either. The excerpt I saw doesn't say exactly which teaching he means. (SL14)

I couldn't reach any Methodist, Pentecostal or Lutheran treatment of Amos 5 to compare.

---

## 3. Other views

- **Critical scholarship (vv. 7–9, 14–15):** The Expositor's Bible thinks vv. 14–15 are probably not in their original position. It also doubts the phrase "the LORD is His name," because that wording doesn't occur elsewhere in the book. Ellicott mentions Ewald moving v. 7 to after v. 9. (EXP; ELL)
- **Old Greek and early church readings:**
  - The Septuagint applies v. 7 to the Lord ("he established righteousness on earth"). (PUL)
  - In v. 15 the Septuagint has the people say "we have hated evil." (PUL)
  - Jerome reads the vineyards of v. 17 as places of joy turned into places of tears. (PUL)
  - Pseudo-Rufinus explains "never to rise again" (v. 2) as a mourner overstating the disaster. (PUL)
- **Word-play note:** Utley explains that the Gilgal pun repeats the same Hebrew verb in a construction that makes it more intense. (UT)

I found nothing on Catholic or Orthodox readings, the NET Bible notes, or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching, because those sources weren't reached. If you start a new session, those are the gaps to fill: the Wesley notes and Lutheran sources would cover the remaining traditions.
